doc.title: James Chirillo interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2007

title: Parents' support and grandfather the Sanitation Department trumpeter
summary: Chirillo's trumpeter grandfather, Navy officer father, first guitars, and parental support as grades and the 1976 State Department tour with the One O'Clock showed his seriousness.

bands.name: New York City Sanitation Department Band

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Well were your parents supportive of your — I assume when you went to North Texas State you were thinking well I’m going to a career in music.

Yeah. I mean my grandfather initially was a professional trumpet player, my dad’s dad. He played the Panamanian Exposition of, what was that, 1908 or something like that. And he met my grandmother and she said, “Look if you want to marry me you’re going to have to get a job. A real job. Typical. And so he was in the New York City Sanitation Department a garbage man. But then after a while, but that was back in the days when the City had, every department had their own band. The Fire Department had their own band, the Police Department, all the departments had their bands. The Sanitation Department had their own band. They even had their own conductor, an Italian conductor. And most of the guys in the band were Italian guys. All this is just to say that they had like some serious training and there was like plenty of time where he wasn’t even like lifting garbage cans anymore, he was just out there playing different events with that band. The ’39 World’s Fair in New York, he was playing the World’s Fair every day. The Queen Mary would come in and he’d go down and play for whoever was coming in on the Queen Mary. So there was a little respect for that already in the family. My father was a career Navy officer and they bought me my first guitar. My brother had an old Sears & Roebuck acoustic archtop and I just ended up beating on it more than him. And when I was 13 my parents bought me a little Vox electric guitar. So you’ve got to say they were supportive, but you know, I was making nothing but pretty savage noise on it back in those days. And when I was being particularly — shall we say — difficult, to put it politely, my old man looked and he says, “What are you going to do with yourself? You ain’t going to do that.” And I said, “I’m planning on doing this with my life.” He says basically you’ve got to be kidding me. I mean because I was just making a lot of noise. But then as he saw I got more and more serious, and of course when I was going to Bellevue Community College and bringing home the grades, and I was taking other music classes there too, then yeah, then I went to North Texas and it was the same thing, I was 3.9 or whatever the heck it was down there too. So yeah, then they knew I was getting serious and I ended up in that One O’clock and you know we toured. We did a State Department tour in 1976 of Russia of the Soviet Union, so we went all over. My first time overseas. A week in Portugal. You know it was great. And I was totally ignorant, I had no idea. But it was highball. And you know, yeah, so I got that scholarship as I had mentioned before. So yeah, they were supportive, absolutely.

Is there some, was there a big break for you when you look back on post-college then, was there a relationship with a particular musician or something that happened that you felt really opened things up?
